newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. businesses urge German economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. businesses urge German economic reforms.

text.p: The American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, which represents local subsidiaries of some of the largest U.S. enterprises, on Friday urged the Bonn government to step up sorely-needed reforms.

Germany must develop a vision and a determination to reform outdated structures and stand up to special interests if it is to keep from falling behind in international competition and create the conditions for lasting economic growth.

Concerned that political parties were dragging their feet about such key reform issues as income and corporate taxes, Chamber president Fred Irwin rejected excessive regulation and conditions that discouraged investment.

"We know that Germany is a good place, but a difficult place to do business," said Irwin as he introduced Chancellor Helmut Kohl to address the 600 executives attending the Chamber's annual meeting in Duesseldorf.
"Laws should be there to promote business and not to get in its way. Whoever wants to create new jobs in Germany must confront this problem," he said.
Irwin said that instead of discussing how to improve conditions to promote the creation of jobs, Germans all too often discussed how to preserve the status quo.
"This discussion is completely wrong," he said.

He underlined the commitment of U.S. companies to Germany, saying that of the 100 largest firms in Germany 12 were owned by American companies and that more than 1,800 U.S. firms accounted for 35 percent of foreign investment in Germany.

Since German unification in 1990, more than 240 U.S. firms had invested over 12 billion marks ($7 billion) in east Germany, helping to rebuild the region after the end of communist rule and securing some 55,000 jobs.

Kohl, days after the collapse of tax talks with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), sought to assure business leaders that the government would not be deterred in its efforts to lower taxes and improve conditions for investment.

"In a word, let me say Germany is a good place to do business but it can still be improved," he said. "You can be assured that there will be an agreement (on taxes) in the upper house. We cannot live any longer with these tax rates."

After collapse of tax talks with the SPD, the government introduced a bill in the lower house of parliament on Friday to cut income taxes up to 30 billion marks in 1999, with some corporate tax cuts planned for 1998.
Dissatisfaction with the pace of German reforms goes beyond taxes, extending into other areas of business such as the deregulation of telecommunications.
Although Germany will open its telecoms markets to full competition in January, there is still no independent regulator and monopoly Deutsche Telekom controls over 90 percent of the telecoms market.
James Bindenagel, acting U.S. Ambassador to Germany, urged Bonn to resolve some of the remaining questions to make it easier for companies to get ready for competition.
"Our complaint is not about not having an independent regulator, but not being able to make business decisions. We encourage the government to complete its reforms," he said.
Ron Sommer, chairman of Deutsche Telekom, said Europe has started well behind the U.S. in opening telecoms markets.
"But in the meantime the signals for open telecommunications markets have also been set here in the Old World," he said. ($ = 1.714 German Marks)
